canonical_policy.name: Swagger documentation must match runtime behavior
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Swagger/OpenAPI metadata must describe the API that actually runs, including routes, important response statuses, schemas, and authentication behavior; do not document speculative responses.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Real running API/no speculative status matches. Whole middleware pipeline, actual-auth scheme with anonymous exemption, useful docs/multiple-document gate, explicit generated contracts and UI verification all separately covered.

context_quotes:
- Swagger/OpenAPI metadata must describe the API that actually runs — routes, important response statuses, schemas and authentication behavior — and must not document speculative responses.
- Default: Swagger UI is enabled in Development and exposed in other environments only when deployment requirements explicitly justify it.

Generate separate or clearly grouped documents per supported version when clients need them (technique: `swagger`); the documented version matches runtime routing and Controller metadata. Versioning does not change normal HTTP semantics (`http-api`).

Accuracy rule: `rules/backend/api.md` § OpenAPI and Swagger — for example, not `201` for an endpoint that returns `200`, not `204` for one that returns a body. Possible responses come from the whole pipeline: model binding, validation, authentication/authorization, rate limiting, centralized exception handling and other middleware, not only explicit action branches; a status that is merely theoretically possible is not documented. For creation, document `201 Created` with `CreatedAtAction`/`CreatedAtRoute` when a canonical URL exists.

When failures use `ProblemDetails`/`ValidationProblemDetails`, describe those contracts where useful. Keep internal exception types, stack traces, SQL, connection strings and filesystem paths out of Swagger examples and descriptions (`rules/backend/error-handling.md` § Unexpected failures).

When the API actually uses authentication, configure the matching security definition and requirements — for Bearer authentication, a Bearer scheme so protected endpoints can be exercised from Swagger UI. An installed authentication package alone is no reason to add a scheme, and global requirements are not applied to anonymous endpoints.

Document what helps consumers: important preconditions, idempotency semantics, pagination/filtering behavior, meaningful outcomes — not descriptions that repeat action or property names. XML comments can help public contracts when the project chooses them; they are not needed on every internal type.

Use several Swagger documents only for a real contract separation, such as API versions (`api-versioning`) or distinct public/internal surfaces.

## Generated clients

When the contract drives Angular or other client generation: treat breaking schema changes seriously, keep response metadata accurate, avoid unstable anonymous response shapes, use explicit request/response contracts and review generated-client changes when the contract changes.

## Verification after API changes

1. Verify Controller behavior.
2. Verify the relevant integration tests.
3. Verify the response metadata.
4. Start the API when the change affects startup or composition.
5. Open the Development Swagger UI and confirm it loads.
6. Exercise representative endpoints through Swagger when that is a meaningful behavioral check, and preserve newly verified behavior in maintained tests (see also: `verify` § 4).

Metadata that disagrees with runtime responses; Swagger UI exposed publicly without a reason; Swagger treated as a substitute for integration tests; global authentication requirements on anonymous endpoints; anonymous objects as long-lived contracts; a second competing documentation stack without a concrete need.

canonical_policy.name: Health checks are cheap and deterministic
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Health checks must remain cheap and deterministic and must not become full business workflows or perform expensive/mutating database work.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Cheap deterministic probes/no mutation match; long timeout/large allocation, no grading system captured. Routine failed-probe Error avoidance alreadyBF0034.

context_quotes:
- Health checks must stay cheap and deterministic and must not become business workflows or perform expensive or mutating database work.
- Liveness must not depend on external dependencies whose unavailability would cause restart loops (by default no database or remote API checks); readiness may depend on capabilities required to serve traffic and must reflect startup completion and required-dependency availability.

A database check is a lightweight connectivity/availability check (`rules/backend/hosting.md` § Health checks); provider integrations help. Check an external dependency only when its availability defines readiness, prefer a lightweight check of the needed capability, and avoid readiness chains (service A → B → C) without understanding their operational consequences.

Probes run frequently: avoid expensive queries, long external timeouts, large allocations, business workflows and Error-level logs for every normal failed probe.

Health checks as a code-quality grading system; database writes or business transactions from probes; every dependency on liveness; expensive queries; secrets or stack traces in payloads; remote dependency chains without operational justification.

canonical_policy.name: Liveness and readiness have distinct dependency semantics
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Liveness should normally avoid external dependencies that could cause restart loops; readiness may depend on capabilities required to serve traffic and should reflect startup/dependency availability appropriately.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Stronger restart-loop exclusion alreadyBF0095. Readiness startup gating, tag/scope, avoid unexamined chains and native HTTP probes with in-container executable verification all recorded.

context_quotes:
- Health checks must stay cheap and deterministic and must not become business workflows or perform expensive or mutating database work.
- Liveness must not depend on external dependencies whose unavailability would cause restart loops (by default no database or remote API checks); readiness may depend on capabilities required to serve traffic and must reflect startup completion and required-dependency availability.
- Publicly reachable health responses must not expose secrets, credentials, connection details, stack traces or unnecessary internal diagnostics.

Expose liveness/readiness through ASP.NET Core health checks (`health-check`) and prefer the orchestrator's native HTTP probes. Runtime images may lack `curl`, `wget` or a shell: if Compose itself runs an in-container health command, verify the executable exists or add a deliberate probe mechanism, weighing the cost of debugging packages in a production image.

SDK image as production runtime; root execution without reason; secrets baked into images; arbitrary infrastructure in Compose; assuming `curl`/`wget` exist; production migrations at application startup (see also: `delivery-pipeline` § 3); specialized image variants without compatibility checks; Docker concerns leaking into Domain/Application code.

Health checks answer whether the running application is alive and/or ready to serve traffic. Distinguish liveness from readiness when the deployment infrastructure benefits from it.

Readiness asks: can this instance currently serve the traffic it is responsible for? Tag the checks that define it, and include only dependencies required for meaningful readiness — an optional external service need not make the whole application unready.

When initialization is asynchronous or slow, keep readiness unhealthy until required startup work completes; using liveness for this causes restart loops.

## Database and external dependencies

A database check is a lightweight connectivity/availability check (`rules/backend/hosting.md` § Health checks); provider integrations help. Check an external dependency only when its availability defines readiness, prefer a lightweight check of the needed capability, and avoid readiness chains (service A → B → C) without understanding their operational consequences.

## Status codes and payloads

Health endpoints return success when healthy and a non-success status when unhealthy under the probe policy; `HealthCheckOptions` maps statuses. Business API status semantics do not transfer mechanically to orchestrator probes. Keep probe responses small; operator-level diagnostic detail goes behind network or authorization controls appropriate to the environment.

## Exposure

Probes usually need to be reachable by infrastructure without user authentication. Options: private/internal network access, a dedicated management port, host restrictions, authorization when the probe infrastructure supports it. Detailed diagnostics are not published unauthenticated on the internet.

## Performance

Probes run frequently: avoid expensive queries, long external timeouts, large allocations, business workflows and Error-level logs for every normal failed probe.

Health checks as a code-quality grading system; database writes or business transactions from probes; every dependency on liveness; expensive queries; secrets or stack traces in payloads; remote dependency chains without operational justification.

canonical_policy.name: Normal client cancellation is not a server failure
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not map normal client-request cancellation to a generic 500 response or log it as an unhandled application failure.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Normal client cancellation not500/error matches; example499 alreadyBF0055 uncertainty, no fresh adoption mandate. Distinguishing request/own/upstream timeout captured0425.

context_quotes: - Normal client-request cancellation is not a server failure: do not map it to a generic 500 response or log it as an unhandled application error.
Centralize unexpected failures in an `IExceptionHandler`, handling client-aborted requests (`HttpContext.RequestAborted`) separately (`rules/backend/error-handling.md` § Cancellation).

| Scenario | Technique |
|---|---|
| Invalid HTTP input | Validation problem response |
| Simple query not found | Application returns `null`; API maps to `404` |
| Several expected business outcomes | Typed outcome or Result |
| Unexpected exception | Global `IExceptionHandler` |
| API failure contract | `ProblemDetails` |
| Straightforward use-case/workflow rule | Application validator / Application Service |
| Non-trivial invariant owned by Domain | Domain enforcement |
| Recoverable external failure | Handle or translate at the boundary |
| Unrecoverable external failure | Propagate to centralized handling |
| Client cancellation | Propagate; not a generic `500` |

**504 Gateway Timeout** — acting as an intermediary, an upstream service did not respond in time. Not every internal `TaskCanceledException` is `504`: distinguish a client-cancelled request, our own operation timing out, and an upstream dependency timing out — the right response depends on which occurred and the role this API plays.
